blocks.title: Why Durable Agents with Workflow Engines matters here

spans.text: Problem statement: An insurance-claims agent must survive retries, approval waits, and worker restarts. The learner's job is not to memorize Durable Agents with Workflow Engines; it is to decide what to build or change, what evidence the system may use, and how to tell whether the change improved recovered workflow rate after restart.

Running case: durable workflow state chart for a claims-processing agent. We will keep this same case through the lesson so each idea has a job: frame the problem, explain the mechanism, choose a design, test the implementation, and decide what to do next.

Before reading on, predict: if the process loses its place after a tool timeout, where would you look first - the input, the state or data, the model boundary, the validation check, or the release process?
The lesson skips definition-drilling and spends its effort on edge cases: state boundaries, hidden coupling, observability gaps, and the evidence that would change a production decision.

items.text: Product framing: Durable Agents with Workflow Engines matters when it changes a user-visible decision, release gate, or operational workflow.
Engineering framing: Durable Agents with Workflow Engines matters when it changes data, state, prompts, model behavior, tools, schemas, traces, or runtime constraints.
Validation framing: the lesson is not complete until the team can measure recovered workflow rate after restart on examples that resemble the real workload.

blocks.title: Fully worked example: durable workflow state chart for a claims-processing agent

spans.text: Scenario: An insurance-claims agent must survive retries, approval waits, and worker restarts. The team wants to improve recovered workflow rate after restart, but it has already seen this failure: the process loses its place after a tool timeout.
Here is the worked artifact at design-review depth: concrete enough to inspect, small enough to build as a thin slice.
Complete worked artifact

items.text: Request: "A returning customer asks about a refund and mentions that they prefer email updates." The agent may remember the communication preference, but it must not store payment fragments, one-time codes, or raw complaint text longer than needed.

Artifact: durable workflow state chart for a claims-processing agent. It contains a memory schema, a write filter, retrieval rules, an escalation rule, and a tiny acceptance test tied to recovered workflow rate after restart.

Worked output: store {customer_id, preference: "email updates", source: "support chat", expires_at: "90 days"}; reject {card digits, passwords, medical details}; retrieve only when the current task is about support follow-up.

spans.text: Complete AI-assistant prompt for this artifact

Role: agent designer. Context: An insurance-claims agent must survive retries, approval waits, and worker restarts. Task: design durable workflow state chart for a claims-processing agent. Include memory or state fields, tool permissions, retrieval rules, human review points, audit logs, and failure tests. Output: {state, allowed_actions, blocked_actions, checks, metric}.
Why this is richer than a definition
The example ties Durable Agents with Workflow Engines to a specific input, output, decision, failure mode, and metric. That is the move you should repeat when applying the lesson to your own system.

blocks.title: Mechanism: the mechanism in the running case

spans.text: Mechanism opens the machinery behind Durable Agents with Workflow Engines. In the running case, the important question is: what exactly changes between the user's request and the final output?
Mechanism means tracking what the agent observes, remembers, decides, acts on, and writes back to state.
Two framings for the same idea

items.text: Plain framing: imagine a reviewer following a checklist. They need to see what came in, what was considered, what was rejected, and why the final answer is safe to use.
Technical framing: imagine a trace. It should expose inputs, state, external evidence, model or algorithm output, validation result, and owner for exceptions.

blocks.title: Case study: what changed after the first review

spans.text: The first prototype works on the demo path. Then a reviewer runs the uncomfortable case: the process loses its place after a tool timeout. The output still looks confident, which is exactly why the lesson needs a richer artifact.

The team does not restart from scratch. It adds one missing control to durable workflow state chart for a claims-processing agent: a stricter input contract, better source metadata, a validation assertion, a human-review edge, a rollback trigger, or an audit log depending on where the failure appeared.

items.text: Decision made: keep the thin slice, but block release until the failure is observable and repeatable.
Evidence added: the artifact now shows the input, intermediate evidence, final output, and pass/fail reason.
Metric promoted: recovered workflow rate after restart becomes part of the release gate instead of a dashboard someone checks later.

spans.text: Case-study takeaway: a useful Durable Agents with Workflow Engines design makes the wrong answer inspectable before it reaches users.

blocks.title: How this breaks in practice

spans.text: The failure mode to keep in view is concrete: the process loses its place after a tool timeout. Use it as a diagnostic lens while reading every design choice.

items.text: The agent remembers the wrong thing, forgets the important thing, or cannot distinguish user preference from sensitive data.
A tool call succeeds technically but changes real-world state without review.
The loop repeats because state was not updated after the last action.
The broad warning sign: recovered workflow rate after restart gets worse even though the final answer or artifact still looks polished.

spans.text: Debugging rule: inspect the earliest place where bad evidence can enter and the latest place where validation should have stopped it.

blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid advanced optimization while the team still cannot reproduce or detect: the process loses its place after a tool timeout.
blocks.ruleOfThumb: Make the failure visible before making the system more sophisticated.

blocks.title: Runnable check: filter memory before writing it
blocks.code:
# Durable Agents with Workflow Engines: memory write gate for the running case.
items = [
    {"kind": "preference", "text": "prefers email updates"},
    {"kind": "secret", "text": "card ends in 4242"},
    {"kind": "task_fact", "text": "refund requested for invoice INV-19"},
]
allowed = {"preference", "task_fact"}

def memory_write_candidates(items):
    return [item for item in items if item["kind"] in allowed]

kept = memory_write_candidates(items)
print([item["kind"] for item in kept])
print("safe to write" if len(kept) == 2 else "review")

spans.text: This is a runnable miniature, not the whole production system. It makes the lesson's contract visible: input, decision rule, output, and a check related to the process loses its place after a tool timeout.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict the list of kept item kinds and the final decision.
predictThenReveal.answer:
It prints:
['preference', 'task_fact']
safe to write

The secret is filtered out before memory write. The point is not this tiny classifier; it is the boundary: memory should have an explicit write policy.
